claims.claim: The Recopilación de Leyes de las Indias was approved by Charles II of Spain through a pragmatic issued in Madrid on May 18, 1680.
claims.verbatim: Approved by **Charles II of Spain** through a pragmatic issued in Madrid on **May 18, 1680**

claims.claim: 3,300 copies of the Recopilación were printed in 1681.
claims.verbatim: 3,300 copies printed in 1681

claims.claim: The Recopilación comprised 4 volumes, 9 books, 218 titles, and roughly 6,385 laws, though some sources give 6,377.
claims.verbatim: **4 volumes, 9 books, 218 titles, 6,385 laws** (some sources say 6,377)

claims.claim: Book Six of the Recopilación, De los Indios, governed laws concerning Indigenous peoples.
claims.verbatim: Indians (*De los Indios*)

claims.claim: The 1542 New Laws were part of the earlier Spanish legislation compiled into the Recopilación and attempted to protect indigenous rights.
claims.verbatim: New Laws (1542) — attempted to protect indigenous rights

claims.claim: No complete English translation of the Recopilación exists; only partial translations of individual books have been made.
claims.verbatim: No complete English translation exists

claims.claim: Book VI of the Recopilación, concerning Indians, was translated by S. Lyman Tyler at the University of Utah in 1980.
claims.verbatim: Book VI ("Concerning the Indians") — translated by S. Lyman Tyler (University of Utah, 1980)

claims.claim: The full Spanish text of the Recopilación remains available on the Internet Archive and Spain's official BOE legal library.
claims.verbatim: **Full Spanish text available:** [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/recopilaciondele02spai_1), [BOE.es](https://www.boe.es/biblioteca_juridica/publicacion.php?id=PUB-LH-1998-62)

claims.claim: A merced was the general Spanish term for a land grant, requiring documentation that the land was uncultivated and free of other claims.
claims.verbatim: **Merced** — the general term for a land grant; required documentation proving land was uncultivated and free of other claims

claims.claim: Community land grants under Spanish law included common lands, or ejidos, set aside for communal use.
claims.verbatim: **Community grants** — included common lands (ejidos) for communal use

claims.claim: Spanish community land grants recognized pastos, or pasture and grazing rights, as a distinct communal right.
claims.verbatim: **Pastos** — pasture/grazing rights

claims.claim: Under Spanish and Mexican law, common lands held by a community could not be sold.
claims.verbatim: Under Spanish and Mexican law, common lands could NOT be sold

claims.claim: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo guaranteed that Mexican property rights would be inviolably respected.
claims.verbatim: inviolably respected
claims.source: Wikipedia: Land grants in NM, GAO Report
claims.anchor: ### What Happened After Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848)

claims.claim: US Surveyors General appointed to confirm Spanish and Mexican land grants had little knowledge of Hispano land practices and customs.
claims.verbatim: little knowledge of Hispano land practices and customs
claims.source: Wikipedia: Land grants in NM, GAO Report
claims.anchor: ### What Happened After Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848)

claims.claim: Congress created the Court of Private Land Claims in 1891, originally intended to last five years but extended repeatedly until 1904.
claims.verbatim: Originally designed to last 5 years; extended repeatedly until 1904

claims.claim: The Court of Private Land Claims heard 301 cases covering over 36 million claimed acres.
claims.verbatim: Court heard **301 cases** involving **over 36 million acres**
claims.source: Federal Judicial Center, NM Legislature background paper

claims.claim: Only 24 percent of the acreage claimed in New Mexico was ultimately awarded by the Court of Private Land Claims.
claims.verbatim: Only 24% of acreage claimed in New Mexico was awarded
claims.source: Federal Judicial Center, NM Legislature background paper

claims.claim: Combining the Surveyor General process and the Court of Private Land Claims, 154 total land grants were confirmed between 1854 and 1904.
claims.verbatim: 154 total grants confirmed through both the Surveyor General process (1854-1891) AND the Court of Private Land Claims (1891-1904)

claims.claim: In United States v. Sandoval (1897), the Supreme Court ruled that pueblo lands remained the property of the sovereign and never belonged to the pueblo as a corporate body.
claims.verbatim: The fee of the lands embraced within the limits of pueblos continued to remain in the sovereign, and never in the pueblo as a corporate body
claims.anchor: ### THE SMOKING GUN: *United States v. Sandoval* (1897)

claims.claim: The San Miguel del Vado land grant was reduced from 315,000 acres to roughly 5,000 acres following the Sandoval ruling.
claims.verbatim: The San Miguel del Vado grant was reduced from **315,000 acres to ~5,000 acres**
claims.source: Santa Fe New Mexican, UNM Digital Repository
claims.anchor: ### THE SMOKING GUN: *United States v. Sandoval* (1897)

claims.claim: At least seven communities, known as the Sandoval Seven, were stripped of their common lands following the 1897 ruling.
claims.verbatim: At least 7 communities stripped of common lands
claims.source: Santa Fe New Mexican, UNM Digital Repository
claims.anchor: ### THE SMOKING GUN: *United States v. Sandoval* (1897)

claims.claim: The Sangre de Cristo Land Grant of 1844 covered roughly one million acres in southern Colorado.
claims.verbatim: Sangre de Cristo Land Grant (1844), ~1 million acres in southern Colorado

claims.claim: In 1863, landowner Charles Beaubien signed a document granting settlers rights to pastures, water, firewood and timber.
claims.verbatim: pastures, water, firewood and timber, always taking care that one does not injure another

claims.claim: In 2002 the Colorado Supreme Court reversed decades of precedent, ruling that descendants of the original 1844 settlers held prescriptive easement rights to grazing, firewood, and timber.
claims.verbatim: Colorado Supreme Court reversed decades of precedent — ruled descendants of original settlers have rights to access for grazing, firewood, and timber through prescriptive easement

claims.claim: After a 2018 appellate ruling upheld the 2002 Lobato decision, over 5,000 additional heirs were identified and given land access rights.
claims.verbatim: Over **5,000 heirs identified** and given access rights

claims.claim: The Spanish legal concept of ejido, communal land that could not be sold, has no direct Anglo-American legal equivalent.
claims.verbatim: **Ejido** — communal land that cannot be sold (no Anglo-American equivalent)

claims.claim: Under Spanish law common lands belonged to the community, but US courts ruled they belonged to the sovereign.
claims.verbatim: **Common lands** — under Spanish law, belonged to the COMMUNITY; US courts ruled they belonged to the SOVEREIGN

claims.claim: A GAO report found the land claims confirmation process was inefficient and caused hardships to claimants.
claims.verbatim: inefficient and caused hardships to claimants
claims.anchor: ### How the Language Barrier Caused Loss

claims.claim: Legislation to clarify land grant communities' traditional-use rights on federal land was reintroduced in April 2025 as Senate Bill 1363.
claims.verbatim: **Reintroduced again April 2025** (S.1363, 119th Congress)

claims.claim: New Mexico recognizes 27 community land grants-mercedes as political subdivisions of the state.
claims.verbatim: New Mexico recognizes **27 community land grants-mercedes as political subdivisions** of the state

claims.claim: A 2004 GAO report on the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo's land claims process offered Congress five options, including land transfers and financial payments.
claims.verbatim: offered 5 options to Congress including land transfers and financial payments
